title: A Promise for the Vow
premise: Paloma Eriksen has spent seven years keeping her heart as carefully as her grandfather kept the lighthouse lamp — lit, but never given away. When a clerical error names her and her estranged first love, Elias Varga, as co-owners of the stubborn orchard she's been quietly tending, the two are forced into a year of shared stewardship neither asked for. As Elias's powerful family moves to seize the land through legal pressure and old debts, Paloma discovers the deed was no accident but her grandfather's dying design to mend what she and Elias broke. To save the orchard, she must testify against the family that once destroyed hers — and finally risk loving Elias in the present tense. They win the orchard, lose the illusion of safety, and choose each other anyway, planting the first new trees together in the final scene.
about_author: Dominic Zhou is a former land surveyor who spent a decade mapping coastal properties before turning to fiction, giving his romances an unusual grounding in deeds, boundaries, and the lines people draw. He writes from a converted boathouse and insists every love story is, at bottom, a property dispute between two hearts.

chapters.title: The Lamp and the Ledger
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Seven years after leaving, Paloma tends her late grandfather's orchard and drafts a novel she'll never finish, keeping love safely in past tense. A registered letter arrives: a deed bearing two names — hers and Elias Varga's. The beat is quiet dread: the past has found a legal foothold in her present.

chapters.title: Two Names on Stubborn Ground
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias returns to the coast to contest the deed, certain his family's lawyers can dissolve it in weeks. Seeing Paloma among the apple rows dismantles his certainty. The beat is reluctant recognition: he came to erase the orchard and finds himself unable to look away from the woman in it.

chapters.title: Terms of Coexistence
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Forced into a provisional co-ownership agreement, they set rules: no past, no feelings, split labor. Pruning season makes liars of them both. The beat is brittle humor curdling into intimacy — every rule they write is a rule they're already breaking.

chapters.title: What the Varga Name Buys
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The Varga family's attorney arrives with a buyout offer and veiled threats, revealing Elias's father financed the original foreclosure that broke Paloma's family. Elias, caught between blood and conscience, refuses to sign. The beat is betrayal reframed — Paloma learns the enemy has been standing beside her all along, choosing her.

chapters.title: Grandfather's Ink
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Searching the lighthouse records, Elias finds Paloma's grandfather deliberately structured the deed as a trap of hope: a co-tenancy that only dissolves if both parties consent, or endures if both stay. He says nothing. The beat is guilty tenderness — Elias now holds the truth that could free them both and fears it will only wound her.

chapters.title: First Frost, First Confession
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. A killing frost forces an all-night salvage of the harvest. Exhausted and lantern-lit, they finally speak the truth of the night they separated seven years ago. The beat is catharsis — old wounds opened deliberately, and for the first time, dressed rather than hidden.

chapters.title: The Family Reckoning
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias confronts his father, offering to trade his inheritance for the orchard's survival. His father counters with a threat aimed at Paloma's livelihood and her grandfather's name. The beat is the cost of belonging — Elias learns that leaving a family of power means being hunted by it.

chapters.title: Lent Pieces
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Terrified of the Vargas' retaliation, Paloma does what she's always done: offers Elias only pieces of herself, pushing him away to protect him. He leaves for the city to fight the legal battle alone. The beat is heartbreak as self-sabotage — she saves him by breaking them both, and hates the arithmetic of it.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. At the ownership hearing, the Vargas' lawyer exposes the grandfather's deed as sentimental engineering. Paloma arrives unannounced and testifies — not for the land, but for the right to choose her own life and her own love in the open. The beat is the climax: the whole heart, risked publicly, and the judge's ruling upholds the deed.

chapters.title: Planting Season
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, closing on both. Spring: the Vargas withdraw, Elias has traded fortune for belonging, and the orchard is theirs in every tense. In the final scene they plant saplings from the oldest tree, and Paloma writes the last line of her novel — a promise, not a vow. The beat is earned peace: love kept not in the past, but in the ground.
